plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. At the end, she asks in return, “Do you want to move on Zhou Gui’s line?”—the old case moves from “putting the two men surnamed Zhou together to investigate the roots of the grain-transport gang” into “Zhou Gui’s personal network itself is also marked with a question, and the right to handle it is handed back to Lu Wenfeng.”

Lu Wenfeng took up the question ‘This line with Zhou Gui—do you want to move on it?’ and first called a stop to that line—‘Don't move. Keep taking his river catch as usual, and don't probe even half a sentence,’ narrowing the task to ‘only record which boat he sat in when he came, and whom he met’; he then shifted the spearhead of inquiry from ‘whether to move on Zhou Gui's line’ to ‘the evidence for Zhou Laosan's death report,’ pressing, ‘Who brought the news of Zhou Laosan's death? Is there anything in Zhou Gui's own hand?’—the old case moved from ‘putting a question mark on the Zhou Gui contact’ into ‘even the evidence for a single death report must be checked down to the level of handwriting.’

Liu Sanniang takes up the question about 'the proof of Zhou Laosan's death,' hands over the proof (a verbal message brought by a boat hand, no letter and no written note, only the line 'Laosan is gone, epidemic disease, buried'), and turns up the flaw in that proof (she never saw that boat hand again afterward and did not even ask his surname); she then infers on her own that 'Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead' and 'Zhou Gui has covered for him for two years,' and throws out the most dangerous layer—'The person he is hiding from may not be Shen Henian. It may also be... me.' At the end, she accepts the task (the next time Zhou Gui comes to deliver fresh river goods, she will not probe or ask, only watch the boat, its direction, and where it goes; the limit is three days, and she will also keep an eye on boats coming from the north for Lu Wenfeng)—the old case moves from 'even the proof of a death notice must be verified down to the handwriting level' into 'the death notice itself may be false, the only remaining living witness from the old escort team may still be alive, and may be hiding from her.'

Lu Wenfeng receives the most dangerous inference—“It’s also possible that he was avoiding me”—first using “He may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s thoughts for him yet” to relieve her self-doubt, turning the threat back from “the old subordinate was avoiding her” to “the old subordinate may have been protecting her.” He then lifts the warm wine and shifts the probing point from “evidence for the news of death” to “That runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” The old case moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be avoiding her” into “everyone who handled this news of death must be identified; even a passing runner whose surname was never asked must have his face pulled back out of memory.”

Liu Sanniang receives the reassurance and follow-up question, dredges up from the incident two years ago the identifiable features of the errand runner who carried the message (in his early thirties, not tall and rather thin, wearing a short gray-cloth outfit, Jiangbei accent, a bluish copper ring on the middle finger of his right hand, seemingly patterned), and on her own links the 'copper ring' with the 'Bronze Crane Ring,' inferring that 'that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian—first confirming that Zhou Laosan was dead, then using this message to seal my mouth.' From there she further infers, 'this booklet, from beginning to end, is an account book he directed and staged himself,' 'this net of his was not woven in just a day or two,' and 'since you seized that page of rubbing, I'm afraid you've already crashed into the net'—the old case advances from 'everyone who handled this death notice must acknowledge it' into 'the broken line from two years ago is reconnected with identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's whole game.'

Cloud-patterned silk gauze is pale in color. On a twelfth-month day at dusk, with lamps lit in the hall, the tabletop was dark and the window ledge bright. A pale handkerchief placed at the edge of the table, seen from across the river, would be just a small bright patch of white. One could see 'there is a handkerchief,' but not 'what kind of handkerchief.'

A grass radical, with a '孙' underneath—it is the character '荪.' Boats in the water towns like to take their names from water plants: duckweed, water chestnut, sweet flag. The character '荪' doesn't stand out. But just so, pressed underneath it is a '孙.'
As for the 'Sheng' mark, the character '盛' has '成' on top and '皿' underneath; it has no grass radical. It was not the same boat, nor the same mark.

When it drifted away, it went north. Follow the current past the north wharf, then another half li upstream; by the water there is a private berth, the warehouse of Second Master Sun's silk and satin shop. Its back door opens right onto the water.
That boat was not passing by. It had gone home.

"Master Lu, I escorted boats for the Canal Gang for more than ten years. On the water, I recognized people and banners; my eyesight is no worse than a man's. plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. At the end, she asks in return, “Do you want to move on Zhou Gui’s line?”—the old case moves from “putting the two men surnamed Zhou together to investigate the roots of the grain-transport gang” into “Zhou Gui’s personal network itself is also marked with a question, and the right to handle it is handed back to Lu Wenfeng.”

Lu Wenfeng took up the question ‘This line with Zhou Gui—do you want to move on it?’ and first called a stop to that line—‘Don't move. Keep taking his river catch as usual, and don't probe even half a sentence,’ narrowing the task to ‘only record which boat he sat in when he came, and whom he met’; he then shifted the spearhead of inquiry from ‘whether to move on Zhou Gui's line’ to ‘the evidence for Zhou Laosan's death report,’ pressing, ‘Who brought the news of Zhou Laosan's death? Is there anything in Zhou Gui's own hand?’—the old case moved from ‘putting a question mark on the Zhou Gui contact’ into ‘even the evidence for a single death report must be checked down to the level of handwriting.’

Liu Sanniang takes up the question about 'the proof of Zhou Laosan's death,' hands over the proof (a verbal message brought by a boat hand, no letter and no written note, only the line 'Laosan is gone, epidemic disease, buried'), and turns up the flaw in that proof (she never saw that boat hand again afterward and did not even ask his surname); she then infers on her own that 'Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead' and 'Zhou Gui has covered for him for two years,' and throws out the most dangerous layer—'The person he is hiding from may not be Shen Henian. It may also be... me.' At the end, she accepts the task (the next time Zhou Gui comes to deliver fresh river goods, she will not probe or ask, only watch the boat, its direction, and where it goes; the limit is three days, and she will also keep an eye on boats coming from the north for Lu Wenfeng)—the old case moves from 'even the proof of a death notice must be verified down to the handwriting level' into 'the death notice itself may be false, the only remaining living witness from the old escort team may still be alive, and may be hiding from her.'

Lu Wenfeng receives the most dangerous inference—“It’s also possible that he was avoiding me”—first using “He may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s thoughts for him yet” to relieve her self-doubt, turning the threat back from “the old subordinate was avoiding her” to “the old subordinate may have been protecting her.” He then lifts the warm wine and shifts the probing point from “evidence for the news of death” to “That runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” The old case moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be avoiding her” into “everyone who handled this news of death must be identified; even a passing runner whose surname was never asked must have his face pulled back out of memory.”

Liu Sanniang receives the reassurance and follow-up question, dredges up from the incident two years ago the identifiable features of the errand runner who carried the message (in his early thirties, not tall and rather thin, wearing a short gray-cloth outfit, Jiangbei accent, a bluish copper ring on the middle finger of his right hand, seemingly patterned), and on her own links the 'copper ring' with the 'Bronze Crane Ring,' inferring that 'that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian—first confirming that Zhou Laosan was dead, then using this message to seal my mouth.' From there she further infers, 'this booklet, from beginning to end, is an account book he directed and staged himself,' 'this net of his was not woven in just a day or two,' and 'since you seized that page of rubbing, I'm afraid you've already crashed into the net'—the old case advances from 'everyone who handled this death notice must acknowledge it' into 'the broken line from two years ago is reconnected with identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's whole game.'

evidence.quote: I tucked the string of keys at my waist a little farther in and nodded.
"He brings his own wine vessel. Every time he comes, he carries an old bamboo basket, with a tin flask inside. He buys the jar and pours it himself when he gets back.

"He pays with his left hand. His right hand—that right hand of his was once twisted by a cable on a boat. The middle finger and ring finger can't straighten; they're bent, and he can't clench it fully.
"A ring... I've never seen him wear one. That right hand of his isn't convenient; he couldn't wear one.

"The day after tomorrow is the eighteenth. We sell wine as usual; A'fu will receive him, and I will be behind the counter doing the accounts. When he comes, I will note the wine vessel, note the hand, note the route. When he leaves—I will see him to the door, and take the chance to look whether that wooden plaque at his waist is still there."

evidence.quote: Don’t see him off. As usual, whoever greets him greets him; do not change the rules in the slightest.
When he competed in bird maneuvers three years ago, were there boats on the river, signal lamps, or people from the Sun family? Do you still remember the shape and style of that wooden tag?

engagement.user_interest_reading: In the previous turn, Liu Sanniang handed over the accessible pretext that Zheng Yazi buys Nü’erhong on every date ending in eight each month, and that “the day after tomorrow is the eighteenth,” and further provided Zheng Yazi’s identifiable features (he brings his own tin flask and bamboo basket, pays with his left hand, his right hand is maimed, he has a wooden tag on his wrist, smells of sandalwood, and three years ago made a bird-spreading-its-wings gesture), substantively advancing Lu Wenfeng’s goal on this trip of sounding things out. In this turn, Lu Wenfeng fixes the mode of contact for her with “Don’t see me off; whoever usually greets him should greet him, and not the slightest rule should be changed” (do not alert him, do not change the person), then narrows the investigation from “boats coming from the north” to the old-acquaintance line of the Sun family warehouse gatekeeper with “When he made the bird gesture three years ago, were there boats on the river, signal lamps, or people from the Sun family?” and “Do you still remember the shape of that wooden tag?” This shows that he has not only taken up her inference, but is also preparing to push this line toward Zheng Yazi and He Pa. Given Lu Wenfeng’s low extraversion, avoidant attachment, and medium engagement_sensitivity, this way of responding—“not pressing about where the information came from, first setting the tone for her, then handing the judgment back”—fits him perfectly. Flat relative to the prior (0.98).
engagement.tolerance_reading: The scene places extremely high demands on the innkeeper's reliability and discretion (standing by the word “trust,” not leaking the movements of guests staying at the inn, and not drawing blades or spilling blood inside the inn). In the previous turn, Liu Sanniang had already handed over Zhou Gui's name, the old Qixia Ferry case, the former escort team's deputy's identity, the old waterway behind the courtyard and the firewood-gate password (three short, one long), the five people who knew the password, and the identities and whereabouts of the remaining three old associates; she had also handed over the “Sheng” character on the stern of the northern cargo boat, Agou the unloading porter, the dog barking in the side alley, and the embroidered-crane handkerchief Sun Jingtang had left behind, as well as the handkerchief's material, embroidery thread, scent, and the identifiable features of the errand boy who carried the message. In this turn, Lu Wenfeng further pushes the questioning to “whether there were boats or lamp signals on the river, or anyone from the Sun family, when he made the bird gesture three years ago” and “the form of that wooden plaque,” which amounts to handing over another layer of the surveillance line on the river three years ago, the old escort-team network, and the people inside the inn who handled the matter, while also putting Second Master Sun, an old acquaintance, on the chopping block. Tolerance dips slightly from the prior 0.14 to 0.13.

plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. At the end, she asks in return, “Do you want to move on Zhou Gui’s line?”—the old case moves from “putting the two men surnamed Zhou together to investigate the roots of the grain-transport gang” into “Zhou Gui’s personal network itself is also marked with a question, and the right to handle it is handed back to Lu Wenfeng.”

Lu Wenfeng took up the question ‘This line with Zhou Gui—do you want to move on it?’ and first called a stop to that line—‘Don't move. Keep taking his river catch as usual, and don't probe even half a sentence,’ narrowing the task to ‘only record which boat he sat in when he came, and whom he met’; he then shifted the spearhead of inquiry from ‘whether to move on Zhou Gui's line’ to ‘the evidence for Zhou Laosan's death report,’ pressing, ‘Who brought the news of Zhou Laosan's death? Is there anything in Zhou Gui's own hand?’—the old case moved from ‘putting a question mark on the Zhou Gui contact’ into ‘even the evidence for a single death report must be checked down to the level of handwriting.’

Liu Sanniang takes up the question about 'the proof of Zhou Laosan's death,' hands over the proof (a verbal message brought by a boat hand, no letter and no written note, only the line 'Laosan is gone, epidemic disease, buried'), and turns up the flaw in that proof (she never saw that boat hand again afterward and did not even ask his surname); she then infers on her own that 'Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead' and 'Zhou Gui has covered for him for two years,' and throws out the most dangerous layer—'The person he is hiding from may not be Shen Henian. It may also be... me.' At the end, she accepts the task (the next time Zhou Gui comes to deliver fresh river goods, she will not probe or ask, only watch the boat, its direction, and where it goes; the limit is three days, and she will also keep an eye on boats coming from the north for Lu Wenfeng)—the old case moves from 'even the proof of a death notice must be verified down to the handwriting level' into 'the death notice itself may be false, the only remaining living witness from the old escort team may still be alive, and may be hiding from her.'

Lu Wenfeng receives the most dangerous inference—“It’s also possible that he was avoiding me”—first using “He may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s thoughts for him yet” to relieve her self-doubt, turning the threat back from “the old subordinate was avoiding her” to “the old subordinate may have been protecting her.” He then lifts the warm wine and shifts the probing point from “evidence for the news of death” to “That runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” The old case moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be avoiding her” into “everyone who handled this news of death must be identified; even a passing runner whose surname was never asked must have his face pulled back out of memory.”

Liu Sanniang receives the reassurance and follow-up question, dredges up from the incident two years ago the identifiable features of the errand runner who carried the message (in his early thirties, not tall and rather thin, wearing a short gray-cloth outfit, Jiangbei accent, a bluish copper ring on the middle finger of his right hand, seemingly patterned), and on her own links the 'copper ring' with the 'Bronze Crane Ring,' inferring that 'that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian—first confirming that Zhou Laosan was dead, then using this message to seal my mouth.' From there she further infers, 'this booklet, from beginning to end, is an account book he directed and staged himself,' 'this net of his was not woven in just a day or two,' and 'since you seized that page of rubbing, I'm afraid you've already crashed into the net'—the old case advances from 'everyone who handled this death notice must acknowledge it' into 'the broken line from two years ago is reconnected with identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's whole game.'
attention: Liu Sanniang: “It may also have been to protect you. Don’t decide the dead man’s intentions for him just yet”—he took up the inference that perhaps even she herself did not dare to think, did not follow the suspicion, and instead found a reason for Zhou Laosan to have been protecting her. When she threw out “the one he was avoiding may also have been me”, she was gripping the wooden wedge, her knuckles turning white; he took it and pressed it down for her, and that well stirred to the bottom became slightly calmer.

Liu Sanniang: “That errand boy who carried the message—do you still remember his appearance, his accent, or any striking object on him?” Immediately after this question, she is pinned back in place again: even that passing errand boy from two years ago, whose surname she never even asked, has to be pulled from memory into some shape for comparison. She can still keep her face steady, but before answering she has to take a breath first.

Liu Sanniang: His line, "It might also be that he was protecting you," took on the most dangerous self-doubt for her; his follow-up question about the shop assistant's appearance is an investigation along the thread. Her coldness and tautness are all directed at "Shen Henian," the "bronze crane ring," and that life-demanding ledger, not at the person in front of her.

Liu Sanniang: His line, “it’s also possible he was protecting you,” was him taking up the inference for her that even she might not have dared to think—she threw out “maybe the one he was avoiding was me,” and he did not follow her into suspicion, but instead found a reason for Zhou Laosan to have been protecting her. This intent to take the burden off her goes one step closer than the previous turn, when he stopped the Zhou Gui thread: last time, what he protected was her line; this time, what he protected was her heart.

Liu Sanniang: The line 'it may also be protecting you' holds down, on her behalf, that urgent impulse to act immediately—she does not have to suppress it herself, and instead becomes steadier. But when asked, 'That runner who passed on the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him?', she first has to run it through her mind: if she answers, it is equivalent to handing over another layer of details about the old escort-team network; if she does not answer, she would be failing the truth he risked his life to bring.

Liu Sanniang: With his line, “he might also be protecting you”, he takes over for her the layer of self-doubt that “Zhou Laosan might be hiding from me as well”—the most dangerous bit of inference she had handed out is received, and that force of “whether to put myself into this” instead twists even tighter: the more he holds it for her, the more she owes him. Immediately after, his question, “That shop assistant who brought the message, do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him?”, again verifies in finer detail the evidence just handed over.

Liu Sanniang: “That runner who carried the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” This question places back into her hand a loose thread that had originally already snapped: that passing runner, whose surname she never even asked, has now become someone who must be identified. Together with the marker “the person wearing a bronze crane ring” and the inference “Zhou Laosan may not be dead,” several loose threads are handed to her at the same time, and she has not yet touched any of them.

Liu Sanniang: “Don’t move. Keep taking his river fish as usual, and don’t probe by even half a sentence”—the only line she can actively use was already sealed off in the previous turn. In this turn, he asks further about the appearance, accent, and conspicuous belongings of the errand hand who carried the message, which is equivalent to asking her to identify, from a memory two years old, a person whose surname she never even asked. Where Shen Henian is now, whose hands the original register fell into, who is wearing the bronze crane ring, and where Zhou Laosan is hiding if he did not die—every single thing is still stuck at the end she cannot reach.

Liu Sanniang: “It may also be protecting you. Don’t decide the dead person’s intentions for him just yet.” This sentence presses back that bit of urgency in her, that “this cannot be delayed.” The other party is watching from the dark; she cannot move, she can only watch. The urgency eases slightly, but this layer remains: if the three characters “Shen Henian” really spread in the north, her twelve years of stability could be overturned at any moment.

Liu Sanniang: In the previous turn she had already handed over the old waterway in the rear courtyard; in this turn, his line “it may also be protecting you” takes on the most dangerous self-doubt for her—what she handed over, he catches, and also holds down for her. This closeness has already moved from “speaking of old matters” to “entrusting the lifeline”; now another layer has been added: “he keeps it for her, and also unburdens her heart for her.”

Liu Sanniang: The room is still her room, and the thread of conversation is still taken up by her—but this turn, his line, “Don’t decide what the dead were thinking just yet,” sets the tone of the judgment for her, and then redirects to “That errand boy who carried the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or anything eye-catching on him?” The inference she handed over has been taken up by the other party and given a new direction, with the rhythm tilting slightly toward him.

Liu Sanniang: The three characters “Shen Henian” have already nailed the mole she had suspected for twelve years from a shadow into a human name, and the previous turn added that “a live witness had been dug up.” In this turn, his line “It may also have been to protect you” is protecting her heart and does not intrude further; but the question “That errand-runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him?” still reaches another layer into her old escort-team connections—even that passing errand-runner from two years ago, whose surname she never even asked, has to be dug out of memory.

Liu Sanniang: No matter how big the matter is, she bears it herself. His line, “It’s also possible he was protecting you,” relieved her of self-doubt, and she accepted it, but she still made her own decisions—whether to answer what that shop hand looked like, and how to pay attention to boats coming from the north, were all things she weighed for herself. Even the inference “the person he was hiding from may also have been me” was something she first thought of herself.

Liu Sanniang: The first page of the ship register has the name of her old escort team, and in the previous turn she also personally told an outsider about ‘the old escort team’s deputy’ and that ‘Zhao Dabangzi was the escort leader.’ She also acknowledged Shen Henian’s handwriting, gave the endings of the two surviving witnesses, and said the maiden name ‘Liu Ruyi.’ In this turn, his line ‘it could also have been protecting you’ amounts to pressing back for her the step of ‘breaking the rules,’ slightly reducing the risk; but with the question ‘That errand boy who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him,’ if she answers, it would nail down the old escort team’s network by another layer.

Liu Sanniang: Right now, the three most important things are still these: protect this regular patron who has returned with bloody business and keep him inside the inn; ask clearly about the whereabouts of the boat register and that “third person’s name”; and then follow the line of “someone in the north is digging up an old case” further downward. In this turn, his sentence “it might also be that he was protecting you” relieves her of self-doubt, and he further asks about the appearance, accent, and conspicuous items of the messenger boy, which effectively makes the information-gathering line concrete and executable—there is now one more person who needs to be identified.

For Liu Sanniang, the word “trust” is the foundation on which she stands, and the line in the back courtyard is even more untouchable. In the previous turn, she had already handed over Zhou Gui, told outsiders about his identity as the old escort team’s deputy, and even proactively proposed using the old waterway in the back courtyard to establish contact. In this turn, his line “It may also be that he is protecting you” effectively presses back down the step in which she would “break the rules,” slightly restoring her defensive position; but the question “That runner who passed on the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or anything conspicuous on him?” still probes another layer into her old escort-team connections.

Lu Wenfeng: She even said something like “the one he’s hiding from might also be me,” and he did not follow that opening to stab into her heart. Instead, he pressed that layer of self-blame back for her—“it may also be that he is protecting you.” The way this place treats him is no longer the relationship of a familiar customer; he is someone they are willing to hand the most dangerous layer to for weighing, and he is able to hold that weight.

Lu Wenfeng: while he presses back for her the thought that “the one being avoided might also be me”, he also fixes his ears on that messenger he has not even asked the surname of—appearance, accent, conspicuous objects, every detail must be dug out. On the surface he is steady reassurance; underneath, that string has not loosened in the slightest.

Lu Wenfeng: She even said, "Maybe the one he was hiding from was me," and he did not seize the chance to press her; instead, he helped press that layer of self-blame back down for her, then lifted the warm wine and asked slowly. The one drawing near is him, and the one he is guarding is still her—but this time, he was the first to loosen an inch for her.

Lu Wenfeng: His sentence “it may also have been protecting you” pressed down on the well overturned in her heart—so perhaps that layer of self-blame, “what he was hiding from was me,” is not necessarily confirmed. But the layer of “if Zhou Laosan is really alive, why has he not contacted me for two years” is still suspended; with this question, he is effectively saying that this line still has to continue downward.

Lu Wenfeng: “It may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide the thoughts of the dead for them yet” — he first held down her self-blame, then lifted the warm wine and slowly asked about the waiter’s appearance and accent. Soothe what should be soothed, pursue what should be pursued—this sense of measure had long been carved into his bones.

Lu Wenfeng: on the one hand, he helped her press back the thought that “the one being avoided might also be me”; on the other, he turned his ear toward that clerk whose surname he had not even asked. The impulse to protect her and the impulse to investigate the case are both at work. On one side are the old escort team’s last remaining contacts and the line in the rear courtyard that must not be exposed; on the other is this familiar old customer before him, someone willing to place her life beside his hand. He has to weigh it until the wine goes cold.

Lu Wenfeng: “That errand runner who brought the message——do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him?”——following the evidentiary loophole uncovered in the previous turn, he pursues this broken line toward identifiable features. If Zhou Laosan is not dead, if Zhou Gui hid something for him, and who that errand runner was——he has not gotten hold of any of these yet, and he needs to keep digging along this path.

Lu Wenfeng: In the previous turn, she answered that of the old escort team only two survivors remained, one who died drunk and one who died of illness, leaving only her; in this turn she answers with the loophole in the evidence for the death report, and throws out “Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead”—which is equivalent to reconnecting this broken line by another segment. The people who can be questioned may have been cut off, but the thread end remains, and may even still be alive.

Lu Wenfeng: “That fellow who carried the message—do you still remember his looks, his accent, or any conspicuous object on him?”—He wants to reconnect this broken thread, which is to say this thread is moving, still stained with human life, and is pressing toward his feet; it cannot be delayed. Yet he still soothes first, then lowers his voice; the sense of urgency is pushed up a notch, but remains under control.

Lu Wenfeng: She even said “the one he’s hiding from might also be me,” yet he did not press the advantage and ask further; instead, he pushed that layer of self-blame back for her before lifting the warm wine and asking slowly. The three words Qixia Ferry are not for just anyone to hear; this distance is no longer that of a regular patron, but of jointly bearing an old case involving human lives.

Lu Wenfeng: His calling a halt to the hidden dock and changing the assignment to 'record only boats and people' means the bargaining chip she handed out has been returned by the other side, and the rhythm tilts slightly toward him; in this turn he first reassures, then follows up by asking about the shop assistant's characteristics, which is equivalent to handing over what to ask next as well. She is in charge here, but this time, he is the one who drew the line first.

Lu Wenfeng: He first pressed back for her the thought that “the one hiding might also be me,” then asked further about the waiter’s features—this is necessary verification for sharing the old case, still probing one layer deeper into her former escort-team connections, but he did not pursue where she came from, nor did he force her to tell the whole story of Qixia Ferry. With this sense of proportion, she cannot fault him.

Lu Wenfeng: he calls off the secret wharf and arranges to ‘keep an eye on boats coming from the north’; she catches that, but still makes her own decisions—whether to answer Zhou Laosan’s evidence of death, and how to keep an eye on boats from the north, are all things she weighs for herself. Even the inference ‘he may also be hiding from me’ is something she herself thinks of first. In this turn he helps her unload self-blame, which is a relief, but when the wine wears off tomorrow morning, he will still have to walk alone.

Lu Wenfeng: “That errand boy who carried the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or anything conspicuous on him?”—following the flaw in the evidence turned up in the previous turn, he pursues this broken thread toward identifiable features. Lu Wenfeng: the matter of staying one night is settled, and his probing words have also been passed to the deepest layer—the rubbings, the contents of the later pages, the clue about the person who bought the register, and the whereabouts of the survivor; he has given all of it to her. evidence: Liu Sanniang actively offers that “on the waterways, fewer and fewer boats drop anchor to rest, while official patrol boats have increased by thirty percent,” going beyond what a simple greeting requires and pointing toward probing for and exchanging information.
Liu Sanniang's persona is that she "can report the dishes while hearing every bit of jianghu rights and wrongs clearly," and she is secretly in contact with former members of the Canal Gang.

Liu Sanniang states Zhou Gui’s name and background, hands over that “over these past six months, someone inside the Cao Gang has sent word north,” and points out that “the tail behind you is probably not just the government’s dog” — exchanging a controllable name for his background; the intent to sound him out remains.

In the room, Liu Sanniang lays out the background of her old escort team and asks in return, “Are there any names of a third person up there?”—her interest in probing is completely ignited by the two words “ship ledger”. She has suspected that ledger for twelve years.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and gives her inferences about his identity, motives, and methods, then immediately asks in return, “Do you still have any sense of what was written on the remaining pages of the original ledger?”—the intent to probe has advanced from “the old case” to “the whereabouts of the original ledger and the people in the north working to overturn the verdict”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian's slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, reveals the outcome that only two survivors remain from the old escort team, and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could help Lu Wenfeng set up a connection to the Cao Gang's hidden wharf—the intent of her inquiry has advanced from "the whereabouts of the original ledger" to "personally making the connection and getting herself involved."

Liu Sanniang digs up the fact that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins, and also uncovers the old suspicion that Zhou Gui is deeply evasive about his cousin-nephew’s death. Liu Sanniang takes up the question of "whether there is anything in Zhou Gui's own handwriting," produces proof of death and then exposes the flaw in that proof, further inferring on her own that "Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead" and "the person he is hiding from might also be me"—the intent to probe has advanced from "personal connections and kinship" to "even the proof behind a death notice must be checked, and even whether an old subordinate survivor is still alive must be weighed."

Lu Wenfeng presses, "That shop hand who carried the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or anything conspicuous on him?"—the intent to probe has advanced from "proof of the death notice" to "even a passing shop hand from two years ago, whose surname you never even asked, must have his likeness dug out of memory."

Liu Sanniang gives the identifiable feature of the errand runner who delivered the message (a copper ring, gone green, with engraved patterns), and on her own merges the “copper ring” line with the “bronze crane ring” line, inferring that “that errand runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian”—the intent to inquire has advanced from “identifying a passing errand runner” to “folding the broken line from two years ago into Shen Henian's whole game”.

paths.summary: Maintain the normal mode of greeting a regular guest; food and lodging are arranged properly. Shen Henian, the bronze crane ring, the convergence of the Zhou-surname thread, evidence of the death notice, the possibility that a survivor still remains, the identity of the errand boy carrying the message, and the topic of watching northbound boats are set aside for now, left until after drinking or the next day.

paths.label: Degrade

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”
