plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. At the end, she asks in return, “Do you want to move on Zhou Gui’s line?”—the old case moves from “putting the two men surnamed Zhou together to investigate the roots of the grain-transport gang” into “Zhou Gui’s personal network itself is also marked with a question, and the right to handle it is handed back to Lu Wenfeng.”

Lu Wenfeng took up the question ‘This line with Zhou Gui—do you want to move on it?’ and first called a stop to that line—‘Don't move. Keep taking his river catch as usual, and don't probe even half a sentence,’ narrowing the task to ‘only record which boat he sat in when he came, and whom he met’; he then shifted the spearhead of inquiry from ‘whether to move on Zhou Gui's line’ to ‘the evidence for Zhou Laosan's death report,’ pressing, ‘Who brought the news of Zhou Laosan's death? Is there anything in Zhou Gui's own hand?’—the old case moved from ‘putting a question mark on the Zhou Gui contact’ into ‘even the evidence for a single death report must be checked down to the level of handwriting.’

Liu Sanniang takes up the question about 'the proof of Zhou Laosan's death,' hands over the proof (a verbal message brought by a boat hand, no letter and no written note, only the line 'Laosan is gone, epidemic disease, buried'), and turns up the flaw in that proof (she never saw that boat hand again afterward and did not even ask his surname); she then infers on her own that 'Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead' and 'Zhou Gui has covered for him for two years,' and throws out the most dangerous layer—'The person he is hiding from may not be Shen Henian. It may also be... me.' At the end, she accepts the task (the next time Zhou Gui comes to deliver fresh river goods, she will not probe or ask, only watch the boat, its direction, and where it goes; the limit is three days, and she will also keep an eye on boats coming from the north for Lu Wenfeng)—the old case moves from 'even the proof of a death notice must be verified down to the handwriting level' into 'the death notice itself may be false, the only remaining living witness from the old escort team may still be alive, and may be hiding from her.'

Lu Wenfeng receives the most dangerous inference—“It’s also possible that he was avoiding me”—first using “He may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s thoughts for him yet” to relieve her self-doubt, turning the threat back from “the old subordinate was avoiding her” to “the old subordinate may have been protecting her.” He then lifts the warm wine and shifts the probing point from “evidence for the news of death” to “That runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” The old case moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be avoiding her” into “everyone who handled this news of death must be identified; even a passing runner whose surname was never asked must have his face pulled back out of memory.”

Liu Sanniang receives the reassurance and follow-up question, dredges up from the incident two years ago the identifiable features of the errand runner who carried the message (in his early thirties, not tall and rather thin, wearing a short gray-cloth outfit, Jiangbei accent, a bluish copper ring on the middle finger of his right hand, seemingly patterned), and on her own links the 'copper ring' with the 'Bronze Crane Ring,' inferring that 'that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian—first confirming that Zhou Laosan was dead, then using this message to seal my mouth.' From there she further infers, 'this booklet, from beginning to end, is an account book he directed and staged himself,' 'this net of his was not woven in just a day or two,' and 'since you seized that page of rubbing, I'm afraid you've already crashed into the net'—the old case advances from 'everyone who handled this death notice must acknowledge it' into 'the broken line from two years ago is reconnected with identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's whole game.'

plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She infers that the later-added name in vermilion means the accountant tampered with the dispatch arrangements; the vital points of dispatching the boat that night, setting the fire, and the signal from the opposite bank were all at the tip of his brush. She then asks in return whether there are any leads in the remaining pages of the original ledger, and points out that Shen Henian left the gang three years ago and was said to have gone north to do silk business—the old case moves from “the mole has a name” into “the mole has an identity, motive, and method, and may still be in the north.”

Lu Wenfeng presses the physical rubbing onto the table for Liu Sanniang to look at first, hands over two new pieces of intelligence—“the later pages are ship orders for a changed route and the whereabouts of the silver” and “the original ledger was bought by someone wearing a bronze crane ring, who has already come south to Jiangnan”—and follows up by asking, “Where are the other two people who survived back then now?” The old case moves from “the inside traitor now has an identity” into “the physical evidence is moving, the pursuers are heading south, and it will draw out the only remaining survivors”; the probing point shifts from “who is the inside traitor” to “where are the survivors”.

Liu Sanniang recognizes Shen Henian’s slender-gold-style handwriting on the rubbing, hands over the fates of the only two survivors left from the old escort team (Zhao Dabangzi got drunk and died at the docks five years ago; Zhou Laosan died of illness back in his hometown two years ago), closes with “Only I’m left—a widow running an inn,” and proactively proposes that the old waterway in the rear courtyard could connect Lu Wenfeng to the Grain Transport Gang’s hidden dock—the old case moves from “where are the living witnesses” into “all the living witnesses are gone, only she remains, and she voluntarily steps beyond her rule of having washed her hands of it.”

Lu Wenfeng calls a halt to the most dangerous line of the dark wharf (“Don’t move for now; the moment you move, you are telling Shen Henian that you still remember the old debts”), narrows the task to “pay attention to ships coming from the north over the past three days, especially people wearing bronze crane rings,” and presses further, “Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui—what is their relationship?”—the old case moves from “all living witnesses have been cut off, and she proactively broke the rules” into “action is narrowed to quiet observation, and the two men surnamed Zhou must be linked together to investigate the root of the canal-transport gang.”

Liu Sanniang receives and pursues the parallel line of questioning, uncovering that Zhou Laosan and Zhou Gui are paternal cousins (Zhou Laosan entered the trade through the guidance of an uncle from the same clan; after that uncle injured his leg, he pushed his nephew forward to fill the vacancy; news of Zhou Laosan’s death was sent through someone by Zhou Gui). She also uncovers an old point of suspicion—over three years, Zhou Gui delivered river delicacies every first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, and though he was loose-tongued, he never mentioned even a word about his cousin. At the end, she asks in return, “Do you want to move on Zhou Gui’s line?”—the old case moves from “putting the two men surnamed Zhou together to investigate the roots of the grain-transport gang” into “Zhou Gui’s personal network itself is also marked with a question, and the right to handle it is handed back to Lu Wenfeng.”

Lu Wenfeng took up the question ‘This line with Zhou Gui—do you want to move on it?’ and first called a stop to that line—‘Don't move. Keep taking his river catch as usual, and don't probe even half a sentence,’ narrowing the task to ‘only record which boat he sat in when he came, and whom he met’; he then shifted the spearhead of inquiry from ‘whether to move on Zhou Gui's line’ to ‘the evidence for Zhou Laosan's death report,’ pressing, ‘Who brought the news of Zhou Laosan's death? Is there anything in Zhou Gui's own hand?’—the old case moved from ‘putting a question mark on the Zhou Gui contact’ into ‘even the evidence for a single death report must be checked down to the level of handwriting.’

Liu Sanniang takes up the question about 'the proof of Zhou Laosan's death,' hands over the proof (a verbal message brought by a boat hand, no letter and no written note, only the line 'Laosan is gone, epidemic disease, buried'), and turns up the flaw in that proof (she never saw that boat hand again afterward and did not even ask his surname); she then infers on her own that 'Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead' and 'Zhou Gui has covered for him for two years,' and throws out the most dangerous layer—'The person he is hiding from may not be Shen Henian. It may also be... me.' At the end, she accepts the task (the next time Zhou Gui comes to deliver fresh river goods, she will not probe or ask, only watch the boat, its direction, and where it goes; the limit is three days, and she will also keep an eye on boats coming from the north for Lu Wenfeng)—the old case moves from 'even the proof of a death notice must be verified down to the handwriting level' into 'the death notice itself may be false, the only remaining living witness from the old escort team may still be alive, and may be hiding from her.'

Lu Wenfeng receives the most dangerous inference—“It’s also possible that he was avoiding me”—first using “He may also have been protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s thoughts for him yet” to relieve her self-doubt, turning the threat back from “the old subordinate was avoiding her” to “the old subordinate may have been protecting her.” He then lifts the warm wine and shifts the probing point from “evidence for the news of death” to “That runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any striking object on him?” The old case moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be avoiding her” into “everyone who handled this news of death must be identified; even a passing runner whose surname was never asked must have his face pulled back out of memory.”

Liu Sanniang receives the reassurance and follow-up question, dredges up from the incident two years ago the identifiable features of the errand runner who carried the message (in his early thirties, not tall and rather thin, wearing a short gray-cloth outfit, Jiangbei accent, a bluish copper ring on the middle finger of his right hand, seemingly patterned), and on her own links the 'copper ring' with the 'Bronze Crane Ring,' inferring that 'that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian—first confirming that Zhou Laosan was dead, then using this message to seal my mouth.' From there she further infers, 'this booklet, from beginning to end, is an account book he directed and staged himself,' 'this net of his was not woven in just a day or two,' and 'since you seized that page of rubbing, I'm afraid you've already crashed into the net'—the old case advances from 'everyone who handled this death notice must acknowledge it' into 'the broken line from two years ago is reconnected with identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's whole game.'

plot_point: Old regular Lu Wenfeng returns after half a year and orders lodging from the proprietor Liu Sanniang—warmed wine, two hot dishes, and a quiet room—exchanging greetings and reminiscing.

Liu Sanniang efficiently makes arrangements: she reserves Tianzi Room No. 1, quotes the old-rule price of five qian of silver, catches the cue of “the wind is tight at the ferry,” offers the fact that patrol boats have increased, and then asks in return, “passing through or staying long-term?”

Lu Wenfeng agrees to stay for one night first and see how the wind blows tomorrow, pays five qian of silver, and the matter of lodging is settled; he then immediately advances the topic from the tense situation at the ferry to whether the official patrol boats have come ashore to ask about people, escalating the probing.

Liu Sanniang puts the silver into the cabinet, tells the truth about going ashore in plain clothes to investigate and the rumors from old Cao Gang members about movements at the northern ferry, reiterates the rule of secrecy, and asks Lu Wenfeng in return about the safety of the northern route—the thread of conversation is caught by her and passed back, and the two sides enter a substantive exchange of movements.

Lu Wenfeng does not answer the question about the Northern Route’s safety, but instead reveals, “They changed horses three times to keep watch on me,” confirming that he is being tailed on this trip; he then asks for the names of the canal gang’s old people, requests that the meal be sent to his room, and, with the phrase “stained with the old blood of Qixia Ferry,” lays the old case from twelve years ago on the table—the topic formally moves from hall-front pleasantries toward a deep conversation in a private room, and probing escalates into a half-offered, half-hidden showdown.

Liu Sanniang accepts the showdown and responds substantively: first she orders a room delivery to separate them from the ears in the hall, then gives the name and background of Zhou Gui, an old member of the Cao Gang, and offers “someone in the Cao Gang is sending word north”. Finally she points out, “this tail behind you is probably not just an official dog”—she trades a controllable name for his bottom line, while shifting the topic from Qixia Ferry to that tail. The showdown enters a two-way exchange.

Lu Wenfeng caught the two-way exchange and handed over another layer: he reported, "I shook the tail clean outside the city," warned, "Don't alert Zhou Gui yet," and then threw out, "That ship register that sank at Qixia Ferry back then has surfaced in the north recently; the first page has the name of your old escort team on it," requesting, "Let's go into the room, close the door, and talk." This directly linked the key physical evidence of the old case to Liu Sanniang's own identity in the old escort team, formally pushing the conversational thread into a closed-door deep discussion.

Liu Sanniang accepts a confidential talk in the inner room with the three words “go upstairs”, leading Lu Wenfeng into Tianzi No. 1 Room: first instructing Afu to watch the hall, then pushing open the window to confirm that no one is under the corridor, formally moving the conversation from the front hall into a private space.

Inside the room, Liu Sanniang gives up the background of her old escort team (five chests of government silver, seven people escorting the boat, three survivors, Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort, and she was the deputy), and asks in return, “Is there perhaps a third person’s name up there?”—the closed-room deep talk moves from “he hands over clues” into a two-way laying bare of “she was there too.”

Lu Wenfeng catches that question, hands over in person the third name written in vermilion on the first page of the ship register, "Shen Henian," and explains that the original register appeared three days ago at Bailang Market in the north, that he only managed to seize a rubbing of one page, and that the person who sold the register died that very night. At the end he asks in return, "Shen Henian—you know him?"—the secret-room deep talk moves from "she was there too" into the deepest layer of "the mole has a name, and the person in the know has already been silenced." The showdown escalates into jointly bearing an old case that carries a human life.

Liu Sanniang acknowledges “Shen Henian” and reveals a new layer: this person was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Grain Transport Gang. On the day before the escort mission, he once advised Zhao Dabangzi to change course to the North Branch, but failed; afterward, citing a leg injury, he did not board the boat and waited ashore to provide support. She turns up the layer of suspicion that Zhou Gui is keeping something deeply hidden and throws out "Zhou Laosan may not necessarily be dead," which can also be explained as protecting an old acquaintance and helping Lu Wenfeng pick up the loose thread, rather than actively collecting intelligence.

Lu Wenfeng first lifts from her the self-blame of “what he was avoiding might also have been me,” which can also be interpreted as protecting an old acquaintance and shielding her heart, rather than deliberately digging deeper.

When she answers with the features of the bronze ring, she leaves room for "I cannot say that is the Crane Ring," which can also be interpreted as protecting the old escort-team network and not making the statement absolute, rather than actively probing deeper.
alternatives: She was merely greeting an old regular, renewing an old acquaintance; the message was passed along as casual small talk, with no intent to probe.
Her attention to “people asking around” and the ship register comes from vigilance about the old case and her own safety, not from actively collecting intelligence.

paths.label: Advance
paths.reasoning_trace: In this turn, Lu Wenfeng first uses "It may also be that he was protecting you. Don’t decide a dead man’s intentions for him yet" to relieve Liu Sanniang of the most dangerous layer of self-doubt in "perhaps the one he was hiding from was me." He then picks up the warm wine and shifts the line of inquiry from "proof of the death report" to "that runner who brought the message—do you still remember his appearance, accent, or any conspicuous object on him?"—returning an originally broken thread to the level of identifiable features. Liu Sanniang has already taken it up, given the feature of the copper ring, and on her own connected the lines to infer that "that runner was scouting the way for Shen Henian" and that "this web of his was not woven in just a day or two." The interaction enters a new situation: the old case changes from "the death report itself is false; the surviving witness may still be alive and may be hiding from her" into "the broken thread from two years ago has been reconnected to identifiable features, and has been incorporated into Shen Henian’s whole game." Liu Sanniang’s persona is "someone who, while listing the dishes, hears the rights and wrongs of the jianghu perfectly clearly"; the back courtyard is precisely a relay point for information, and that runner was someone she personally dealt with two years ago. Since she has already told an outsider the old story with her own mouth, and has personally broken the rule of washing her hands of the matter, now that even the evidence for this broken thread has been checked and found flawed, she instead owes him one more measure, and it is even harder for her to swallow back that unsaid piece. Since he has already handed over four things—physical evidence, content, direction of flow, and a surviving witness—and has helped her hold down the most dangerous line, what remains depends on how the conversation goes this night.
requirements: Liu Sanniang gives whatever memory details she can about "that errand boy who passed the message" (appearance, accent, conspicuous object), or continues on with "where would Zhou Laosan be hiding if he didn't die," "who was Zhou Gui covering for, and who gave him a reason he had no choice but to hide it for."

The two sides exchange the pieces each has grasped regarding "who the person wearing the bronze crane ring is," "what is written on the other pages of the original register," "where Shen Henian is now," and "who in the north is digging into this old case."

Liu Sanniang, with the briskness of an innkeeper, steers the topic toward the Caobang mole, the people from the north trying to overturn the case, or that bronze crane ring, and implements the matter of "keeping an eye on boats coming from the north" (how to watch, through whom, and when to report).
paths.summary: The private in-depth conversation moves from “the news of death itself is false; a survivor may still exist and may be hiding from her” into “the broken lead from two years ago has been reconnected to identifiable features and folded into Shen Henian's entire game.” Shen Henian, Bailang Market, the death of the account-book seller, the buyer of the bronze crane ring, the connection between Zhou Gui and Zhou Laosan, and the identity of the shop assistant who carried the message become threads shared by both sides, advancing both relationship and information.

original.rationale: This fits Liu Sanniang’s dual goals of sounding out the situation and protecting familiar customers, and also fits Lu Wenfeng’s purpose of wrapping serious business in an old acquaintance. The topic has already been passed by both sides to physical evidence, flow direction, surviving witnesses, parallel-line questioning, personal networks and kinship, quietly observing the assignment, proof of the death report, the possibility that a surviving witness is still alive, identifiable features of the errand boy who carried the message, and the layer where the bronze ring and the bronze crane ring run in parallel. The initiative lies in whether to answer what that errand boy looked like, how to keep an eye on boats coming from the north, and what to ask next.

paths.label: Maintain
paths.reasoning_trace: Liu Sanniang suppresses the surging emotions with a shopkeeper’s skill—Zhou Gui has already been handed over, the tail has been pointed out, the boat register has been heard, the old escort team’s background has been disclosed, the three characters Shen Henian have entered their ears, the rubbing has been seen, the survivor’s outcome has been answered, the line for making contact has been given, the secret pier has been called off, the Zhou-family kinship has been dug out, proof of death has been handed over, the inference that a survivor may still be alive has been thrown out, the errand waiter’s features have been given, and the bronze ring and crane ring have been connected into one line. Next she only needs to arrange for wine and dishes to be served and settle their food and lodging, temporarily setting aside “who that waiter is” and “whether Zhou Laosan is really dead” with “we’ll talk tomorrow” or “let me think about it.” Both sides maintain the normal pattern of greeting familiar regulars; the topic is touched on and then stopped, left for after drinking or for the next day. Lu Wenfeng sees that she does not take the deeper thread, and does not force her; he only holds the bowl and drinks slowly—that matter weighs heavily, and he had already wanted to mull it over for another night.
requirements: Liu Sanniang glosses over the follow-up about "that shop assistant who brought the message" with polite scene-setting words, without immediately probing deeper.
Lu Wenfeng does not probe deeply, instead arranging food and wine on the table and settling food and lodging.
paths.summary: Maintain the normal mode of greeting a regular guest; food and lodging are arranged properly. Shen Henian, the bronze crane ring, the convergence of the Zhou-surname thread, evidence of the death notice, the possibility that a survivor still remains, the identity of the errand boy carrying the message, and the topic of watching northbound boats are set aside for now, left until after drinking or the next day.

original.rationale: Liu Sanniang observes the rules and is wary of Qixia Ferry; if a guest is unwilling to speak, she does not pursue it. Lu Wenfeng’s matter weighs heavily, and even the old acquaintance and the timing are things she still wants to weigh for another night.

paths.label: Degrade
paths.reasoning_trace: If Liu Sanniang, because the question about “the shop assistant who carried the message” touches on old matters she personally handled two years ago, completely shuts her mouth, or if Lu Wenfeng, because of the unfamiliar faces in the hall and his fatigue, no longer follows up, then the hints and questions both sides have offered all fall flat. The pleasantries sink into repetitive courtesy, leaving only the routine exchange of serving dishes and wine, with no progress in either acquaintance or information.
requirements: Liu Sanniang avoids answering or gives an irrelevant answer to this layer of follow-up about “the errand boy who passed along the message”.
Lu Wenfeng no longer follows up; both sides fall silent separately.
paths.summary: The small talk lapsed into mere courtesies, the probing fell flat, and neither the relationship nor the information made any progress.

a few days ago, an old hand from the Grain Transport Gang got drunk and started bragging. He said the northern ferry crossings haven't been peaceful since autumn began, as if there have been some troop movements.
questions: Master Lu, on this trip back, are you passing through, or—staying for a while?

fabricated_items: That man's surname is Zhou, given name Gui. He used to run outer-river boats for the Grain Transport Gang. Three years ago he washed his hands of the trade, and now he ferries people at the downstream crossing. His mouth is loose, but his heart is solid—when he's drunk he likes to brag, but things he shouldn't say will rot in his belly before he spits them out.
over the past half year, someone inside the Grain Transport Gang sent word north. Zhou Gui's level couldn't find out exactly what it was about.
On that escort run of mine, we were carrying five chests of official silver and two rolls of official documents. There were seven brothers escorting the boat. Three came back alive.

The first page of the boat register was the roster of the escort leaders—if that thing truly surfaced, the first page should have the signature and seal of the man who led the escort. My sworn brother Zhao Dabangzi was the lead escort. I was his deputy.
questions: Who fished it up, where did it appear, and on it—was there still a third person’s name?

fabricated_items: Shen Henian was originally the accountant of the Qixia Ferry branch of the Canal Gang

Shen Henian was not on the boat that night. After the incident, he said his leg injury had kept him from boarding, and that he was waiting onshore to receive us
seven men went into the water to save the goods, and of the three who came back alive, two were pulled up from the bank by him
Shen Henian withdrew from the Canal Gang three years ago. I heard he went north to do silk business
questions: Master Lu, you only managed to seize one page of a rubbing. Do you still have any idea what was written on the remaining pages of the original register?

fabricated_items: Zhao Dabangzi—drank himself to death by the docks five years ago. The authorities examined him and said he slipped and fell into the water.

The remaining one was called Zhou Laosan. Back then he was the helmsman on the boat. After Qixia Ferry, he was scared out of his wits and went back to his hometown to farm. Two years ago, I asked someone to inquire about him; the village said he had caught a plague and was gone.

back when Zhou Laosan entered the trade, it was an uncle from his own clan who showed him the way. That uncle used to run short-haul routes for the Grain Transport Gang in his early years; later, after injuring his leg, he pushed his nephew up to fill the vacancy
Zhou Gui is Zhou Laosan's cousin-uncle

The year Zhou Laosan returned to his hometown to farm, Zhou Gui was still running boats for the Grain Transport Gang. When I heard the news of Zhou Laosan's death, it was Zhou Gui who had someone send word—he said it was an epidemic, and that the village buried him in such a hurry they did not even have time to prepare a coffin

these past three years, Zhou Gui has been ferrying downstream, and on the first and fifteenth of every month he sends a load of fresh river catch to my shop. He has a loose tongue and loves gossiping about this household and that, but he has never mentioned so much as half a word about that nephew of his
questions: This Zhou Gui lead—do you want to move on it?

I can’t remember his face very clearly, but he wore a ring on the middle finger of his right hand. It was copper, greenish in color, and there seemed to be some pattern engraved on it.”

There are only three money shops in this city that can exchange loose silver: Jubao on East Street, Wanchang by the bridgehead, and Old Song's by the docks

of the Canal Gang old hands still alive today, there are five in total who know the signal for that hidden passage in my rear courtyard. Zhou Gui is one. Zhao Dabangzi, who is dead, was one. There are three more

Before the twelfth lunar month last year, Second Master Sun's silk shop took in a batch of raw silk from the north. They said it had been transferred over from Bailang Market. I heard Sister Wu mention it once—the next door to her tofu shop is a cloth stall, and the stall owner complained that the batch of silk was of good quality, but the price had been pressed too low, throwing the local silk market into disorder.
when he left, he smiled at me and said, 'Sanniang, the days ahead won't be peaceful. Keep your door well guarded.'
a character 'Sheng' painted on the stern, red characters on a black background

When Second Master Sun left that day, he left something on the table—a handkerchief, folded square, with a crane embroidered on the corner
That handkerchief... is still pressed in my cabinet now
The material is cloud-patterned gauze from the north—light, soft, translucent. Jiangnan cannot weave this kind of quality

The embroidery thread is Su embroidery silk, but the stitching is wrong—Su embroidery values evenness, neatness, fineness, and density, yet the stitches of this crane pattern are slanted upward, like the handiwork of a northern embroideress
The smell... … Only a faint medicinal smell is left—like angelica mixed with dried tangerine peel

Second Master Sun never used things with crane patterns before. That man cared about show; what he used were all round longevity patterns and ruyi patterns, auspicious ones. The crane is a solitary bird. He did not like it
Shen Henian was different. His name contains the character for crane. In his early years in the gang, a seal he carried with him and a folding fan were both engraved with cranes. I have seen them
a black-awning cargo boat, with no registration plate and no banner raised. Its bow sat low, its draft deep, as if it carried heavy cargo
There was someone crouching at the bow wearing a bamboo hat; I couldn’t see his face clearly, but he was facing this way the whole time—toward this window
After Second Master Sun left, that boat stayed for almost another half hour before leaving. When it left, it did not pole off; it drifted with the current, northward.

every month on dates with an eight, Zheng the Mute comes to my shop to buy a jar of nu'er hong. The day after tomorrow is the eighteenth.
